title: Reported speech: statements
tagline: Telling someone what somebody else said, without quoting their exact words.
why: Telling someone what another person said — without quoting their exact words — is something B1 Preliminary tests in the reading cloze and expects in a Writing Part 2 story with dialogue. Getting say and tell right, and remembering to move the tense back one step, are two of the most common things that let B1 students down.

hook.text: Nadia is writing for the school newspaper. She interviewed Miss Vega, who said, "I love teaching science." Nadia writes: Miss Vega said (that) she loved teaching science. Mateo: "Why did love become loved?"
hook.ask: Compare Miss Vega's exact words with Nadia's sentence in the newspaper. What changed: the verb tense, the pronoun, or both?

diagrams.title: Direct speech → reported speech

before.text: "I love teaching science," said Miss Vega.

after.text: Miss Vega said (that) she loved teaching science.

steps: Remove the quotation marks and change the pronoun (I → she).
Move the main verb one step back into the past (love → loved).

rows.label: With to
cells: She said to me that she was tired.
NOT tell to — never use to after tell

steps.label: Past simple → past perfect
steps.ex: "I saw the film" → she said she had seen the film.

head: Direct speech
Reported speech
Example
rows: "I like pizza." → She said she liked pizza.
"I'm studying." → He said he was studying.
"I saw it." → She said she had seen it.
"I'll call you." → He said he'd call me.
"I can swim." → She said she could swim.

examples.text: Miss Vega said (that) she loved teaching science.
examples.note: say — no person needed after it

examples.text: Miss Vega told us (that) she loved teaching science.
examples.note: tell + person — never tell to someone

examples.text: Nadia said to me that the interview went well.
examples.note: say to + person is possible, but told me is more natural

examples.text: "I write for the newspaper," Nadia said. → Nadia said she wrote for the newspaper.
"I'm working on an article," she said. → She said she was working on an article.
"I interviewed the head teacher," she said. → She said she had interviewed the head teacher.
"I'll finish it tonight," she said. → She said she'd finish it that night.
"My article is ready," said Nadia. → Nadia said her article was ready.
examples.note: my → her, matching the new subject

examples.text: "I'll post it tomorrow," she said. → She said she'd post it the next day.
examples.note: tomorrow → the next day, because time has passed

examples.text: "I left it here," she said. → She said she had left it there.
examples.note: here → there, because we've moved away from that place

examples.text: "The Earth goes round the Sun," said Miss Vega. → She said the Earth goes round the Sun.
examples.note: a fact that's still true — the tense can stay the same

examples.text: "I love pizza," said Liam. → Liam said he loves pizza.
examples.note: still true now, so the tense doesn't have to change

examples.text: "The meeting is on Friday," said Miss Vega. → Miss Vega said the meeting is on Friday.
examples.note: still relevant — no need to move it back

watch_out.wrong: She told that she was tired.
watch_out.right: She said (that) she was tired. / She told me (that) she was tired.
watch_out.why: tell always needs a person after it; say doesn't.

watch_out.wrong: She said me that she was busy.
watch_out.right: She told me that she was busy.
watch_out.why: say + me is wrong — use tell + person, or say to me.

watch_out.wrong: He said he will call later.
watch_out.why: will moves back to would in reported speech.
Most verbs move back one step into the past when you report them.

watch_out.wrong: He said he saw the film tomorrow.
watch_out.right: He said he had seen the film the day before.
watch_out.why: Time words like tomorrow change too, and a finished past action moves to the past perfect.

watch_out.wrong: Nadia said me she loved the interview.
watch_out.right: Nadia told me she loved the interview.
watch_out.why: Same mix-up: told + person, never said + person without to.

l1.wrong: She said me that she was tired.
l1.why: Spanish me dijo becomes told me in English — say never takes a direct object like that.

l1.wrong: He said he will come tomorrow.
l1.right: He said he would come the next day.
l1.why: will moves back to would, and tomorrow changes to the next day once time has passed.

l1.es: Dijo que le gustaba la pizza.
l1.why: The reported verb usually moves one step into the past, even though Spanish keeps the imperfect unchanged.

l1.es: Dijo que había visto la película.
l1.wrong: She said she saw the film.
l1.right: She said she had seen the film.
l1.why: A past action reported later moves back to the past perfect (had + participle).

l1.es: Me contó que su hermana vivía aquí.
l1.wrong: He told that his sister lived here.
l1.right: He told me (that) his sister lived there.
l1.why: tell needs a person (me), and here changes to there when you're not in that place anymore.

remember.trick: Say has no one, tell always needs someone!
remember.tip: Whenever you report a statement, ask: does the tense need to step back one, and does the time word need to change too?

dialogue.title: Interview for the newspaper
dialogue.context: Nadia is writing the school newspaper article and reports back to Sofia and Liam what Miss Vega told her in the interview.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Miss Vega told me she loved teaching science here.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Really? What else did she say?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: She said (that) she had studied in Arequipa before she came to Lima.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Did she talk about the science fair?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Yes — she said she'd help us organise it next month.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And the new lab? I heard it's opening soon.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: She told us it would open in October.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Did she say why she became a teacher?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: She said she had always wanted to inspire young scientists.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That's a great quote for the article!

items.sentence: "I love pizza," said Liam. → Liam said he ___ pizza.
items.why: present simple moves to past simple

items.sentence: She ___ me that she was tired.
items.why: tell needs a person straight after it

items.sentence: "I saw the film," she said. → She said she ___ the film.
items.why: past simple moves to past perfect

items.why: present continuous moves to past continuous

She ___ (that) the Earth goes round the Sun.

can_do: I can report what someone said, choosing correctly between say and tell.
I can move the tense one step back when I report a statement (present → past, will → would…).
I can change pronouns, times and places correctly when I report speech (tomorrow → the next day).
summary: say has no person after it (or say to + person); tell always needs a person.
Most tenses move one step back: present → past, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could.
Pronouns change to match the new speaker (I → she/he); tomorrow → the next day, here → there.
Facts that are still true can keep the same tense.
that after say/told is optional — the sentence works with or without it.
